title: Season Two, Episode 9: Every Class is a Reading Class 16, 2026
author: Rebecca Birch
source: Chalk Dust (podcast, cross-posted via Rebecca Birch - On Education, Substack), September
summary: Show notes for a Chalk Dust podcast episode in which hosts Rebecca Birch and Nathaniel Swain interview Andrew McCrorey, an instructional leader at Monterey Secondary College in Frankston North, Victoria, about integrating trauma-informed practice with explicit instruction in a highly disadvantaged secondary setting. The central argument is that trauma-informed support and high academic expectations are not in tension: consistent, tightly rehearsed routines function as an equity strategy, freeing teachers from constantly resetting behavior so they can concentrate on instruction. McCrorey walks through specific mechanisms - rehearsed entry routines, a four-to-one ratio of positive to corrective feedback, explicit teaching of behavioral expectations for situations like arriving late, and a universal 'tracking the speaker' attention routine - that together produce predictable classroom environments. The episode also covers literacy-specific techniques, including secondary choral reading for fluency and confidence, cold calling preceded by paired rehearsal time to protect equity of participation, and gist statements as a bridge from reading to written comprehension. Throughout, the guiding claim is that reading aloud and full classroom participation are entitlements for every student, not privileges reserved for the already-compliant or already-fluent.
points: Argues that consistency of routines across a school functions as an equity lever, since predictable expectations reduce the cognitive and emotional load that disproportionately falls on disadvantaged students.
Details a four-to-one positive-to-corrective feedback ratio and scripted entry routines as concrete mechanisms for building calm, fast-starting lessons without lowering academic demands.
Recommends pairing cold calling with prior rehearsal time (e.g., paired think time) so accountability for participation does not become a source of anxiety or inequity.
Presents secondary choral reading and gist statements as explicit-instruction techniques for building reading fluency and comprehension in older students, not only early readers.
Frames explicit teaching of behavioral routines, such as what to do when arriving late, as reducing uncertainty and protecting instructional time rather than functioning as a punitive add-on.
quotes: In this episode of Chalk Dust, Rebecca Birch and Nathaniel Swain are joined by Andrew McCrorey, an experienced educator and instructional leader at Monterey Secondary College in Victoria. Drawing on classroom footage from a secondary setting serving a highly disadvantaged community, Andrew demonstrates how explicit instruction, trauma-informed positive education and high expectations can work together rather than compete with one another.

The discussion explores entry routines, co-regulation, secondary choral reading, gist statements, cold calling, participation as an equity issue, and the explicit teaching of behaviour expectations. Andrew explains how consistency across classrooms can function as an equity strategy, creating predictable environments in which students know what success looks like and teachers can focus on teaching rather than repeatedly resetting behaviour.

Across the episode, Rebecca, Nathaniel and Andrew return to the idea that supporting students does not require lowering the bar. Instead, effective practice combines strong relationships, clear routines, deliberate participation structures and carefully sequenced academic support. The result is a classroom where students are both safe and challenged, and where literacy, behaviour and wellbeing are treated as interconnected parts of successful teaching.

A tightly rehearsed lesson-entry process in which students know what materials to collect, where to go and what task to begin. Andrew explains how predictable entry routines support regulation, reduce bottlenecks and maximise learning time.

Students read a text aloud together, following the teacher's pacing and expression. Andrew uses choral reading in secondary English to build fluency, confidence, prosody and participation while allowing the teacher to hear and correct reading in real time.

Rather than relying on broad classroom rules, Andrew teaches specific routines for situations such as arriving late. Students are shown what to do, what to expect, and how consequences will work, reducing uncertainty and preserving learning time.
